questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question assesses practical knowledge of traffic management in multi-tenant environments. It tests understanding of Istio's traffic splitting capabilities, header-based routing, and safe rollout strategies. Candidates must balance per-tenant isolation against system complexity.

## Key Concepts

- **Istio traffic management**: DestinationRules define service subsets; VirtualServices handle routing rules
- **Canary deployments**: Gradually shift traffic between versions to validate changes safely
- **Header-based routing**: Use x-cluster-local headers or custom headers like X-TENANT-ID to identify tenants
- **Weight-based traffic splitting**: Distribute traffic percentages across subsets

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway-dr
spec:
  host: cnf-gateway
  subsets:
  - name: prod
    labels:
      version: prod
  - name: canary
    labels:
      version: canary
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway-vs
spec:
  hosts:
  - cnf-gateway
  http:
  - match:
    - headers:
        x-tenant-id:
          exact: canary
    route:
    - destination:
        host: cnf-gateway
        subset: canary
      weight: 15
    - destination:
        host: cnf-gateway
        subset: prod
      weight: 85
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: cnf-gateway
        subset: prod
```

```yaml
  name: canary-test

  replicas: 1

    matchLabels:

    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cnf-gateway
        version: prod
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: gateway
        image: cnf-gateway:v1
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
---

metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: canary-test
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
  selector:
    app: cnf-gateway
```

## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical skills in implementing controlled, observable deployments in a multi-tenant CNF gateway environment. It checks familiarity with canary strategies, per-tenant isolation, and metric-driven promotion/rollback.

## Key Concepts

- Canary deployments with Argo Rollouts
- Per-tenant traffic shaping and isolation
- Prometheus-based SLIs and analysis templates
- Automated rollback and promotion thresholds
- End-to-end testing in a single-tenant namespace before broader rollout

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: gateway-rollout-tenant-a
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: gateway
      tenant: a
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: gateway
        tenant: a
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: gateway
        image: registry.example.com/cnf/gateway:latest
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
      - setWeight: 10
      - pause: { duration: 5m }
      - setWeight: 100
      analysis:
        templates:
        - templateName: canary-metrics
        metrics:
        - name: latency
          interval: 30s
          successCondition: result < 0.001 * 0.15
        - name: error-rate
          interval: 30s
          successCondition: result < 0.005
```

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: canary-metrics
spec:
  metrics:
  - name: latency
    provider:
      prometheus:
        url: http://prometheus.k8s.svc
        query: sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_sum[5m])) / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))
  - name: error-rate
    provider:
      prometheus:
        url: http://prometheus.k8s.svc
        query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{status!~"2.."}[5m]))
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adapt this for cross-cluster canaries?
- What monitoring dashboards would you expose to operators for this flow?

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates your ability to design end-to-end provenance controls for CNF environments, specifically addressing how key rotation impacts SBOM generation and policy enforcement in multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters.

## Key Concepts
- Cosign image signing with KMS-backed keys
- SPDX SBOM generation and attestation workflows
- Kyverno policy enforcement for signature and SBOM validation
- Key rotation impact on image provenance chains
- Namespace-scoped testing strategies and rollback procedures

## Code Example
```bash
# Sign image with KMS-backed key
cosign sign --key kms://mykms/path/to/key \
  --attachment sbom \
  registry.example.com/cnf:latest

# Generate and attach SBOM
syft registry.example.com/cnf:latest \
  -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx

cosign attest --key kms://mykms/path/to/key \
  --type spdx --predicate sbom.spdx \
  registry.example.com/cnf:latest
```

## Implementation Strategy
Deploy this solution progressively: start with image signing, add SBOM generation, implement Kyverno policies, then automate the key rotation workflow. Test in isolated namespaces before cluster-wide deployment.

## Why This Is Asked
Assesses ability to design end-to-end supply chain security and runtime integrity for multi-cloud CNFs, including identity management, attestation mechanisms, policy-as-code enforcement, and network isolation during zero-downtime upgrades.

## Key Concepts
- SPIFFE/SPIRE identity management
- TPM/IMA runtime attestation
- SPDX SBOM delta validation
- OPA/Kyverno policy enforcement
- Cilium eBPF network policies
- Canary upgrade strategies

## Code Example
```yaml
# SPIFFE identity configuration
apiVersion: spiffe.example/v1
kind: SPIFFEIdentity
metadata:
  name: cnf-identity-01
spec:
  spiffeID: spiffe://cluster/ns/cnf-01
  parentID: spiffe://cluster/ns/workload-scheduler
  ttl: 1h
```

```yaml
# OPA upgrade gate policy
package cnf.upgrade
default allow = false

allow {
  input.attestation.trust_score >= 80
  input.sbom.delta.additions == 0
  input.network_policy.isolated == true
}
```

## Implementation Approach
The solution integrates identity, attestation, and policy enforcement to ensure upgrades maintain security posture while achieving zero downtime through controlled canary deployments.

```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (yaml)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8simageprovenance
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sImageProvenance
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8simageprovenance
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        input.review.kind.kind == "Deployment"
        some c in input.review.object.spec.template.spec.containers
        not startswith(c.image, "ghcr.io/")
        msg := "image provenance missing or not tenant-approved"
      }
```

```yaml
# Constraint (yaml)
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sImageProvenance
metadata:
  name: per-tenant-provenance
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
  parameters:
    allowedTenant: "tenant-a"
```

```yaml
# Compliant Deployment (yaml)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: tenant-a-gateway
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: gateway
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: gateway
        image: ghcr.io/tenant-a/gateway:v1.0.0
```

```yaml
# Noncompliant Deployment (yaml)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: tenant-a-gateway-bad
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: gateway
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: gateway
        image: unsigned/gateway:latest
```

```bash
# Kubectl steps (one namespace first)
kubectl create ns tenant-a
# 1) Register constraint template and constraint
kubectl apply -f k8simageprovenance_template.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8simageprovenance_constraint.yaml
# 2) Sign and SBOM-attach a valid image (tenant-a key)
cosign sign --key cosign-tenant-a.key ghcr.io/tenant-a/gateway:v1.0.0
# 3) Deploy compliant manifest
kubectl apply -f compliant-deploy.yaml -n tenant-a
# 4) Deploy noncompliant manifest (unsigned)
kubectl apply -f noncompliant-deploy.yaml -n tenant-a
# 5) Check Gatekeeper denials and logs
kubectl get events -n tenant-a
kubectl describe deployment tenant-a-gateway-bad -n tenant-a
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question assesses the ability to design token rotation mechanisms for multi-tenant CNF environments, focusing on atomic secret updates, race condition avoidance, and end-to-end validation.

## Key Concepts
- Ephemeral credentials with TTL management
- Atomic updates using compare-and-swap (CAS) patterns
- Kubernetes Secrets lifecycle management
- Observability of credential rotation events

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: tenant-a-cred
  namespace: cnf-tenant-a
type: Opaque
data:
  token: <base64-encoded-token>
```
